The second step is to check whether the boundary file can be parsed and previewed: bin/coastctl boundary preview --case-dir EXEC.demo --json This command only prints the preview and does not write additional files. You should see something like COAST_BOUNDARY_PREVIEW_JSON, patchCount, the name, type and selector of each patch. If you want to save the preview results to the calculation example directory so that the graphical auxiliary interface or others can view them, you can run: bin/coastctl boundary preview --case-dir EXEC.demo --write --json After execution, EXEC.demo/boundary_preview.json is usually written out. Note: --write will modify your working example directory, so do not run EXEC_TEMPLATE directly. The third step is to check the grid status: bin/coastctl mesh status --case-dir EXEC.demo --json You should pay attention to: Whether the number of ranks is consistent with the number of mpirun -np you plan to run; Whether the required mesh, tile or runtime mesh file can be found; If the geometry or mesh is changed, is it prompted that it needs to be regenerated or there is a mismatch? If you are in the full development workspace instead of the packaged version directory, you can usually replace bin/coastctl with: ./coastctl case validate --case-dir EXEC --json ./coastctl boundary preview --case-dir EXEC --json ./coastctl mesh status --case-dir EXEC --json
title: COAST User Manual

content: 3.15 Contents that are not recommended for novices to modify The following are not absolutely impossible to change, but it is recommended that novices should not explore on their own: Chemical reaction mechanism name, such as arm2, fuel name, species list. Core physical models such as LES, PDF, micro-hybrid, and compressible models in input.d. Geometric units, fluid/solid notation conventions, mesh authoritative source in ibm_mesh.d. The number of ranks in mesh_decomposition and forced splitting, unless you know how to match the run rank and restart files. targetMarker in boundary_conditions.d, unless you explicitly know the numerical boundary path corresponding to the target marker. Spray coupling switch in spray.d, unless the study is a spray study. Restart/, Decomp/, runtime_mesh/ internal files. The current detailed chemical production default for the Methane/ARM2 study is still: chemistry_integrator dvode chemistry_rhs_backend coast_legacy chemistry_jacobian_backend internal_finite_difference chemistry_dvode_mf 22 There is already a generated_sparse_accumulated + mf=21 comparison backend in the program, but 2026-06-26 Hot benchmarks show no production performance benefit, so don’t run it as the default setting. To do development comparison, first read SRC.Coast/docs/CHEMISTRY_PERFORMANCE_OPTIMIZATION_GUIDE.md and EXEC/monitor/chemistry_stage1_benchmark.md. If you encounter any uncertainty, change one parameter first and do a short test and check. Do not change many items at once. 4. Boundary condition settings Boundary conditions determine “where the fluid comes in, where it goes out, and what happens when it hits the wall.” In COAST’s clean EXEC workflow, it is recommended to only modify the entrance, exit and wall through boundary_conditions.d, and do not modify the Fortran source code or the old entrance profile file.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 4.1 What are entrance, exit and wall? You can first understand it in a daily life way: Inlet inlet: where the fluid enters the calculation area. You need to tell COAST the speed, temperature, pressure reference, gas composition, such as air inlet or methane inlet. Outlet outlet: The place where the fluid leaves the calculation area. You usually want to give an outlet pressure and indicate what temperature and composition to use as a reference if local backflow occurs. Wall wall: solid boundary. You need to indicate whether the wall velocity is zero, adiabatic, fixed temperature, and using a wall function. A combustion chamber study usually has at least: one or more air inlets; one or more fuel inlets; an exit; External and internal geometric walls.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 4.2 Basic structure of boundary_conditions.d boundary_conditions.d consists of a set of patches. Each patch describes a type of boundary area, such as main_air, methane_ring, outlet, external_adiabatic_walls. The minimum structure is as follows: version 1; patch main_air { kind inlet; type fixedVelocityInlet; enabled true; allowEmpty false; priority 10; selector { source externalBoundary; side west; marker any; region all; } targetMarker -1; U fixedValue (0 8.0 0); T fixedValue 295; p fixedValue 100000; composition volumeFraction { O2 0.21; N2 0.79; normalize true; } } Explained item by item: version 1;: Boundary file format version. patch main_air: Define a boundary block named main_air. The name must be unique. kind inlet;: This is the entrance. Can also be outlet or wall. type fixedVelocityInlet;: Entry type, here means directly given speed. enabled true;: Enable this patch. Setting to false is equivalent to temporarily disabling it. allowEmpty false;: Do not allow this patch to select even one side. Entrances and exits should usually be left false. priority 10;: priority. When multiple patches overlap, the one with higher priority is applied later and can overwrite the patch with lower priority. selector { ... }: Select which boundary faces belong to this patch. targetMarker -1;: COAST marker written after selection. It affects which boundary processing path the solver uses. U: speed, unit m/s. T: temperature, unit K. p: pressure, unit Pa. composition: gas composition. NOTE: Most lines must have a semicolon ; at the end. Missing semicolons and mismatched braces are the most common formatting errors.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 4.3 selector: Which piece of boundary to choose? selector is the most easily misspelled and most important part of the boundary file. It answers a question: To which mesh boundary surfaces should this patch be applied? Common fields are as follows: Field Function Common writing methods source Where to choose surface externalBoundary, ibmSurface side On which side of the border or grid west, east, left, right, south, north, all marker / markers What the original legacy marker must be marker -1;, markers (-5 -50);, marker any; region Filter by geometric region on the selected side all, box, cylinderRing patchGeometry Use additional patch STL files to assist identification patchGeometry 'Geometry/patches/air_inlet_ymin.stl'; patchTriangles Use recognized triangle patch numbers Usually generated by graphical interface or sidecar cadFaceIds Use CAD/B-rep face numbers Require reliable CAD face id source externalBoundary represents the external computational domain boundary, such as the entire entrance plane, exit plane, and shell boundary. source ibmSurface represents a fluid-adjacent wall surface that already exists near the IBM geometry, such as a spout or wall identified on the STL internal geometry. It cannot create openings out of thin air. The name of side comes from the grid generation and calculation example convention. Don’t just guess based on the map orientation. Currently, the comments for some GTMC-type studies state that side west is the low y entrance and side east is the high y exit; another study may be different. The most reliable way is to look at the existing boundary_conditions.d comments, mesh preview and boundary preview. marker any means “the original marker is not required to be a certain value”. It’s convenient, but also dangerous. This is only recommended when the coordinate range is very narrow and source and side are sufficiently clear. Otherwise, a patch may select faces that it should not select.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 4.4 What is the difference between coordinate selection boundary and patch/STL boundary? COAST supports two common boundary selection methods. The first is patch/STL or CAD markup selection. It relies on additional geometry tags such as: patchGeometry 'Geometry/patches/air_inlet_ymin.stl'; This means “mark the air inlet area with this little STL file”. If the geometry is well provided, this approach is intuitive and the graphical auxiliary interface can more easily display the corresponding areas. Similarly, CAD/B-rep meshes can be used: cadFaceIds (43); This means using CAD face numbering. This should only be written if runtime_mesh/cad_faces.dat or the geometry description explicitly tells you which physical boundary the face id corresponds to. The second category is coordinate selection. It does not rely on patch STL, but uses boundary sides, coordinate range, and radius range to select. For example: selector { source externalBoundary; side west; marker any; region cylinderRing; axis y; center (0 0); radiusRange (0.0 0.03); axialCoordinate y; axialRange (-1.0e30 1.0e30); } This means that on the west side outer boundary, select a circular area around the y axis with a radius from 0 to 0.03 meters. The difference between the two can be recorded as follows: How What to rely on Advantages Risks patch/STL or CAD face Reliable geometry tags, patch STL, CAD face id Clear physical meaning, suitable for graphical interface click If the label is missing, the path is wrong, or the face id changes, it will be empty Coordinate selection Coordinate axis, boundary side, radius or box range No need to patch STL, suitable for STL calculation examples without labels If the coordinate axis, unit, and range are written incorrectly, the wrong selection or empty selection will be made Note: patch STL is an “auxiliary tag” and is not a required condition. Without patch STL, coordinate selection is the officially supported notation.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 4.5 How to set by coordinates when there is no patch STL When the calculation example has only one overall STL and no separate entry/exit patch STL, you can write the boundary as follows. The first step is to determine whether the boundary is an external boundary or an IBM surface: Domain outside entrance, domain outside exit, outside border wall: usually use source externalBoundary. STL internal geometric surfaces, spouts or walls near immersion boundaries: may use source ibmSurface. The second step is to determine the side. If it is an external boundary, it must be as clear as possible which side it is. Don’t use side all for entry/exit in the first place. side all is more suitable for wall patches like “all outer walls”. The third step is to select the geometric area. Select the entire side: region all; Select a rectangular range: region box; bounds (-0.01 0.01 -0.02 0.02 -0.005 0.005); The six numbers of bounds are: (xmin xmax ymin ymax zmin zmax) Choose a circle, donut, or spout ring: region cylinderRing; axis y; center (0 0); radiusRange (0.0069 0.0081); axialCoordinate y; axialRange (-0.00825 -0.00775); Here axis y means that the axis of the ring is y, and the radius is calculated in the plane perpendicular to y. center (0 0) represents the coordinates of the center of the circle in this radial plane. For axis y, the radius is usually calculated from x and z. The fourth step is to set allowEmpty. Entry and exit recommendations: allowEmpty false; In this way, if you cannot select any boundary faces, you will be reminded during the inspection phase instead of running silently. Only certain optional wall patches are available: allowEmpty true; Step five, preview. Coordinate selection without patch STL can also be previewed: bin/coastctl boundary preview --case-dir EXEC.demo --write --json You should see this in the output: nonPatchStlCoordinateSelectorsSupported is true; name, kind, type of each patch; Coordinate rules in selector; If you already have grid check data, you may also see matchedFaces, empty, area, averageNormal.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 4.6 How to write speed, temperature, pressure and composition
title: COAST User Manual

content: Speed U The unit of velocity is m/s, and the three-dimensional vector is written as: U fixedValue (0 8.0 0); The three numbers are x, y, z direction speed respectively. The above represents the velocity in the positive y direction, with magnitude 8 m/s. If the flow direction is negative, write a negative number: U fixedValue (0 -8.0 0); Note: The entrance velocity direction must be consistent with the calculation example coordinates. Don’t just look at “left in, right out”, make sure the actual axial direction is x, y or z. Some IBM portals can use model velocity direction, for example: U model wallNormalIntoFluid; U fixedValue (1 0 0); In the fixed velocity entry, this type of writing means that the velocity direction is determined by the normal direction of the wall, fixedValue Mainly provides speed size. In the mass flow entry, the velocity is automatically converted by massFlowRate, fixedValue only needs to be a non-zero direction seed. Novices should not change the ordinary entrance to this model at will. Unless the existing calculation example has been written in this way, or the developer explicitly requires it.
title: COAST User Manual

content: Temperature T The unit of temperature is K, which is Kelvin: T fixedValue 295; 295 K is approximately 22 degrees Celsius. Do not write the temperature in Celsius directly. For example, if you want to write 25 degrees Celsius, you should write about 298, not 25.
title: COAST User Manual

content: Pressure p The unit of pressure is Pa: p fixedValue 100000; 100000 Pa is approximately one standard atmosphere. The p in the inlet is often used as the reference pressure; the p in the outlet is usually more critical because it controls the pressure reference at the open boundary.
title: COAST User Manual

content: Component composition For ordinary users, it is recommended to use volume fraction: composition volumeFraction { O2 0.21; N2 0.79; normalize true; } This represents an air volume fraction of 21% oxygen and 79% nitrogen. normalize true means allowing the program to normalize the proportions to avoid the sum not being 1 due to decimal errors. For pure methane we can write: composition volumeFraction { CH4 1.0; normalize true; } Quality score is also supported: composition massFraction { CH4 0.055; O2 0.220; N2 0.725; normalize true; } Note: Species names are case-sensitive and must be consistent with the current chemical mechanism. Common effective gas phase species in the current methane/ARM2 calculation example are: CH4 O2 N2 CO2 CO H2O H2 OH O H Cannot be written as ch4, o2, Nitrogen, AIR. If the species is not present in the mechanism, the run will fail during the check or startup phase.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 4.7 Methane/Air Boundary Example Below is a simplified methane/air example focusing on how to write it. Real studies should have their own coordinates, radii, sides and existing file comments. Assumptions: The mainstream direction is positive y; Air enters from the low y outer boundary; Methane is injected from an IBM geometric ring; exit at high y outer boundary; Air temperature and methane temperature are both 295 K; Reference pressure is 100000 Pa. version 1; patch main_air { kind inlet; type fixedVelocityInlet; enabled true; allowEmpty false; priority 10; selector { source externalBoundary; side west; marker any; region cylinderRing; axis y; center (0 0); radiusRange (0.0 0.03); axialCoordinate y; axialRange (-1.0e30 1.0e30); } targetMarker -1; U fixedValue (0 8.0 0); T fixedValue 295; p fixedValue 100000; composition volumeFraction { O2 0.21; N2 0.79; normalize true; } } patch methane_ring { kind inlet; type fixedVelocityInlet; enabled true; allowEmpty false; priority 20; selector { source ibmSurface; side all; marker any; region cylinderRing; axis y; center (0 0); radiusRange (0.0069 0.0081); axialCoordinate y; axialRange (-0.00825 -0.00775); } targetMarker -1; U model wallNormalIntoFluid; U fixedValue (40.0 0 0); T fixedValue 295; p fixedValue 100000; composition volumeFraction { CH4 1.0; normalize true; } } patch outlet { kind outlet; type relaxedPressureOutlet; enabled true; allowEmpty false; priority 10; selector { source externalBoundary; side east; marker any; region all; } targetMarker -2; p fixedValue 100000; backflow { normalFraction 0.1; tangentialDamping 0.8; scalarBlend 0.1; T fixedValue 295; composition volumeFraction { O2 0.21; N2 0.79; normalize true; } } } patch external_adiabatic_walls { kind wall; type noSlipAdiabaticWall; enabled true; priority 5; selector { source externalBoundary; side all; markers (-5 -50); region all; } targetMarker -5; U fixedValue (0 0 0); thermal adiabatic; species zeroGradient; } There are two entries in this example: main_air is the air inlet, priority 10; methane_ring is the methane ring entrance, priority 20, if it overlaps with a wider air region, it will be applied later. Note: side west/east, radius and y range in the example are not universal constants. The scaling example must be adjusted based on geometry and preview.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 4.8 Common entrance types When the velocity is known, use fixedVelocityInlet: kind inlet; type fixedVelocityInlet; U fixedValue (0 8.0 0); T fixedValue 295; p fixedValue 100000; When the total mass flow rate is known, massFlowInlet can be used: kind inlet; type massFlowInlet; massFlowRate fixedValue 0.06; U fixedValue (0 1 0); T fixedValue 295; p fixedValue 100000; Pressure-driven inlets can use totalPressureInlet: kind inlet; type totalPressureInlet; totalPressure fixedValue 101325; U fixedValue (0 1 0); T fixedValue 295; Newcomers are given priority to use the entry types already used in existing calculations. If the original file uses fixedVelocityInlet and you just want to change the speed, don’t change it to another type.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 4.9 Common export types A more reliable relaxation pressure outlet is commonly used in compressible combustion calculations: kind outlet; type relaxedPressureOutlet; targetMarker -2; p fixedValue 100000; If using a fixed static pressure outlet, you may see: kind outlet; type pressureOutlet; targetMarker -60; p fixedValue 100000; Exits also often come with a backflow block. What it means is: If a backflow occurs locally at the outlet, COAST needs to know the reference temperature and composition of the return air or gas. For example: backflow { normalFraction 0.1; tangentialDamping 0.8; scalarBlend 0.1; T fixedValue 295; composition volumeFraction { O2 0.21; N2 0.79; normalize true; } } Novices generally only need to confirm that p, T and the return flow components are reasonable, and do not change the damping coefficient at will.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 4.10 Common wall types Adiabatic no-slip wall: kind wall; type noSlipAdiabaticWall; targetMarker -5; U fixedValue (0 0 0); thermal adiabatic; species zeroGradient; It can be understood that the solid wall does not move, the fluid velocity on the wall is 0, and the wall does not actively give or take away heat. Fixed temperature no-slip wall: kind wall; type noSlipIsothermalWall; targetMarker -4; U fixedValue (0 0 0); thermal isothermal; T fixedValue 500; species zeroGradient; It can be understood that the wall does not move and the wall temperature is fixed at 500 K. IBM wall function wall: kind wall; type wallFunctionAdiabaticWall; selector { source ibmSurface; region all; } targetMarker -5; U model wallFunction; thermal adiabatic; species zeroGradient; wallFunction { enabled true; dampingEnabled true; targetCfl 0.01; maxMultiplier 20; } This type of wall is usually prepared for near-wall processing with complex geometries and high Reynolds numbers. Newbies should not delete existing ibm_wall_function unless you know for sure that this study no longer uses IBM walls.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 4.11 Boundary preview and graphical interface auxiliary files After modifying boundary_conditions.d, run: bin/coastctl boundary preview --case-dir EXEC.demo --json If you just want to see the terminal output, use the above command. If you want a GUI or other tool to read the preview file, run: bin/coastctl boundary preview --case-dir EXEC.demo --write --json After execution, something similar to this will be written in the calculation example directory: EXEC.demo/boundary_preview.json Highlights from the preview: Is patchCount equal to the number of patches you expect; Whether the name of each patch is unique; Whether kind and type conform to the physical meaning; If patchGeometryExists is false, it means that the STL file pointed to by patchGeometry does not exist; If empty is true, it means that the patch is not selected; If matchedFaces is 0, it usually means there is a problem with the selector coordinates, side, marker or geometry label; Whether area and averageNormal roughly match the entrance/exit area and direction expectations. Graphical auxiliary interface Semi-automatic boundary processes may also use sidecars: bin/coastctl boundary sidecar --case-dir EXEC.demo --write --json This command will generate: EXEC.demo/boundary_patch_manifest.json It is an intermediate format between graphical interfaces and border DSL. Usually the user does not need to write it by hand. If you generate a boundary draft from a sidecar, you can run: bin/coastctl boundary write-dsl --case-dir EXEC.demo --json By default, it will be written as boundary_conditions.generated.d and will not directly overwrite the current boundary_conditions.d. Use --apply only when you explicitly want to replace it; when using --apply, the tool will back up the original file first. Note: The automatically generated draft also requires manual inspection of speed, temperature, pressure, composition and coordinate range, and cannot be directly put into formal calculation after being generated.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 4.12 Complete checking sequence after modifying the boundary It is recommended to follow this order: Save boundary_conditions.d. Make a border preview. Check the calculation example configuration. Do a grid status check. Do a test run of very short steps. The first three commands are: bin/coastctl boundary preview --case-dir EXEC.demo --write --json bin/coastctl case validate --case-dir EXEC.demo --json bin/coastctl mesh status --case-dir EXEC.demo --json If an error occurs, do not run the solver yet. Prioritize fixing boundary files and mesh status. For short tests, you can first change lstep in input.d to a smaller value, such as 20 to 50 steps. The short test can be started, the log has no obvious boundary errors, the Visit output can be turned on, and the official steps can be restored.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 4.13 Common bugs and fixes
title: COAST User Manual

content: Error 1: No patch can be selected. Performance: empty is true in the preview; matchedFaces is 0; The boundary is empty when the run is started. Common reasons: side is written incorrectly; source externalBoundary and source ibmSurface are used reversely; The radius or coordinate range is too narrow; STL units are mm, but you understand the coordinates in a scale other than m; marker is too restrictive; patchGeometry path does not exist. Correction method: Check the patchGeometry path first; Confirm which side the entrance/exit is based on the grid preview; Moderately relax the coordinate range; If you really don’t know the original marker, you can temporarily use marker any in a very narrow coordinate range; Do not directly change the entry allowEmpty to true to eliminate errors.
title: COAST User Manual

content: Error 2: The entrance direction is written backwards Performance: The speed near the entrance runs from inside the domain to the outside; The mass flow direction is wrong; The position of the flame or mixing zone is obviously abnormal. Correction method: Confirm whether the mainstream direction is x, y or z; Use positive numbers in the positive direction and negative numbers in the negative direction; For IBM normal entrance, the U model wallNormalIntoFluid writing method in the original file is preferred.
title: COAST User Manual

content: Mistake 3: Temperature unit is written in degrees Celsius Wrong writing: T fixedValue 25; Correct way to write: T fixedValue 298; COAST uses K here. Writing the temperature too low will lead to unreasonable density, reaction and stability.
title: COAST User Manual

content: Error 4: Wrong species name Wrong writing: composition volumeFraction { ch4 1.0; normalize true; } Correct way to write: composition volumeFraction { CH4 1.0; normalize true; } Species names are case-sensitive. Currently, methane/ARM2 commonly uses CH4, O2, and N2, not ch4, oxygen, and air.
title: COAST User Manual

content: Error 5: The sum of the components is unreasonable If using: normalize false; Then the sum of the components should be very close to 1. Newbies are advised to use: normalize true; Writing O2 21; N2 79; can also be normalized for this type of ratio, but it is still recommended to write it directly as 0.21 and 0.79, which is more clear.
title: COAST User Manual

content: Error 6: The patch priority causes the coverage relationship to be reversed For example, a large air inlet covers the entire inlet face, with small methane rings located within it. If the air patch had a higher priority, it might cover the methane ring. Correction method: Use a lower priority for large-scale patches, such as priority 10;; Small-scale patches that need to be covered use a higher priority, such as priority 20;; The patch name must be unique.
title: COAST User Manual

content: Mistake 7: Treating boundary files as hole-drilling tools boundary_conditions.d can only select existing fluid boundary surfaces and assign values. It cannot turn a solid element into a fluid, nor can it open a new spout out of thin air on the STL wall. If you need to add new internal entrances or exits, it is usually the mesh/IBM settings that need to be changed, such as geometry, opening faces, forced blocking planes, etc. This belongs to ibm_mesh.d and the mesh generation process, and cannot be solved by changing the boundary patch alone.
title: COAST User Manual

content: Error 8: targetMarker can be changed at will targetMarker looks like just a number, but it affects which boundary processing path COAST takes internally. Common conventions include: -1: common fixed entry path; -2 or -60: common exit paths, which one to use depends on the calculation example; -5, -50: common adiabatic/zero gradient walls; -4, -40: common fixed temperature walls; -3: common slip or symmetry boundary. When novices only change speed, temperature, pressure and components, do not change targetMarker casually.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 4.14 Self-check list before and after boundary modification Before submission or official operation, you can confirm item by item: Each patch name is unique. Each entry and exit has allowEmpty false. Each entry has U, T, p, composition. Outlet pressure p is reasonable, return flow T and composition are reasonable. The wall type matches thermal, for example thermal adiabatic is used for insulating walls. The unit of velocity is m/s, the unit of temperature is K, and the unit of pressure is Pa. Species names belong to current chemical mechanisms. The coordinate range unit is meters and is consistent with the calculation domain after STL unit conversion. The patch/STL path exists, or confirm that the patch is a pure coordinate selection. The priority of small-scale patches is higher than that of large-scale patches. There are no obvious errors in coastctl boundary preview, case validate, and mesh status. After completing these checks, enter the “Operational Calculation” chapter for short tests and formal calculations. 5. Run the calculation This chapter starts from “preparing to start calculation” to “how to see it when it is running”. If you are using COAST for the first time, don’t rush into long formal calculations. The recommended sequence is: do the pre-operation inspection first, then do the short test, and then do the formal calculation after passing the short test; if the formal calculation is interrupted or needs to be continued, follow the continued calculation process. The following commands are executed in the portable package root directory by default, which is the directory where bin/coastctl, bin/coast-ui, and EXEC_TEMPLATE can be seen. Assume that your working example directory is called EXEC.demo. Note: If you have installed the portable version using install.sh and have executed source "$HOME/.local/coast/env/coast-env.sh", bin/coastctl in the command can be written as coastctl. If you haven’t installed it yet and are just running it directly from the unzipped directory, continue using bin/coastctl.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 5.1 Before starting the calculation, confirm which directory you are in. A COAST calculation does not only run one file, but reads a “calculation directory”. This directory usually contains: The main solver is provided by bin/coast-solver in the package directory; the calculation example directory mainly saves input, grid, restart data and output results; input.d: total control file, which contains whether to read Restart, total number of steps, output frequency, etc.; boundary_conditions.d: boundary conditions such as entrance, exit, wall, etc.; ibm_mesh.d: geometry, mesh, IBM related settings; vtk_output.d: Result output field settings; runtime_mesh/: runtime mesh; Restart/: Restart file for continued calculation; Visit/: post-processing result file; screen: Solver screen log; stdout/stderr and run manifest are placed outside the calculation in .coast_run_logs/ by coastctl, and the specific path is viewed through coastctl monitor. If you are starting from a template, you should copy EXEC_TEMPLATE first and do not calculate it directly in the template: cp -a EXEC_TEMPLATE EXEC.demo Execution location: root directory of the portable package. After execution, you should see: There is an additional EXEC.demo folder in the current directory. In the future, modification, operation, and viewing results will all be based on EXEC.demo, and EXEC_TEMPLATE will remain as it is, making it easier to re-create clean calculation examples in the future. Note: Do not put multiple different tasks in the same EXEC.demo and mix them for a long time. It is recommended to copy a new calculation example directory for each experiment and each working condition, such as EXEC.case01, EXEC.case02.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 5.2 Pre-run checklist The purpose of the pre-run check is not to “formally run a few commands”, but to discover the most common problems in advance: the program does not exist, MPI cannot be started, the input file is written incorrectly, the boundary cannot be selected, the number of grids and restarts does not match, etc. Formal calculations are often time-consuming, and the sooner problems are discovered, the more time is saved. It is recommended to check in the following order.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 5.2.1 Check the running environment bin/coastctl doctor --case-dir EXEC.demo --json Execution location: root directory of the portable package. This command will check: Whether the current directory is a COAST workspace or portable package; Whether the calculation example directory exists; Whether the main solver can be executed; Whether mpirun can be found; Whether python3 can be found; Whether boundary_conditions.d exists; runtime_mesh/ whether there is mesh information; Whether the number of restart.NNN in Restart/ is reasonable; If restart_pdf.NNN exists, whether the number matches restart.NNN; Whether the rank numbers of Decomp/, Restart/ and runtime_mesh/ obviously conflict. After execution you should see: a piece of JSON text. Novices don’t need to fully understand JSON, just focus on "ok": true or "ok": true in each check item. If an item is false, process this item first and do not continue to calculate. Note: Passing doctor does not mean that the physical settings must be correct. It only confirms “whether it can start normally” and “whether there are any obvious gaps in the file structure”.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 5.2.2 Check input file format bin/coastctl case validate --case-dir EXEC.demo --json Execution location: root directory of the portable package. This command will check whether the direct input file of the calculation can be recognized by the tool, especially suitable for running after you have modified the *.d file. After execution, you should see: The JSON shows that the check was successful. If it fails, it is usually because a file is missing, the path is wrong, the field format is wrong, or there is a configuration issue clearly pointed out by the tool. Fix it first, then rerun the command.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 5.2.3 Check whether the boundary condition can be selected bin/coastctl boundary preview --case-dir EXEC.demo --write --json Execution location: root directory of the portable package. This command will read boundary_conditions.d and generate a boundary preview file, which usually reads: EXEC.demo/boundary_preview.json After execution, you should see that each entrance, exit, and wall patch can be parsed. Focus on obvious empty selections, disabled items, spelling errors, or coordinate range errors. Note: Boundary conditions can only “assign physical meaning” to existing boundaries and cannot harden the interior of a solid into a fluid inlet. If an entry cannot be selected, it is usually necessary to check the geometry, grid or coordinate range first, rather than just changing kind to something else.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 5.2.4 Check grid status bin/coastctl mesh status --case-dir EXEC.demo --json Execution location: root directory of the portable package. This command will summarize the runtime mesh of the current study, such as the mesh source, the number of mesh blocks, the geometry file, and whether there are any relationships between Restart and the mesh that need attention. After execution, you should see: There is information such as activeRuntimeMesh, and the rank number and grid file are not empty. If you plan to continue the calculation, pay special attention to whether the current runtime_mesh/ matches Restart/runtime_mesh/.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 5.2.5 Schedule a run, but don’t actually start it yet bin/coastctl run --case-dir EXEC.demo --ranks 128 --preflight --write --json Execution location: root directory of the portable package. The meaning of this command is: run according to the 128-rank plan and do pre-start checks, but do not actually start long-term calculations. It will write the plan and run-control status to the calculation external .coast_run_logs/. Do not leave a .json control file in the EXEC.demo root directory. The specific path can be viewed through the stdoutLog, stderrLog and manifest fields of coastctl monitor: .coast_run_logs/<case>/<run>/coast_run_plan.json .coast_run_logs/_state/<case-key>.json After execution, you should see: "status": "planned" in JSON, and the command will contain: mpirun -np 128 ../bin/coast-solver Note: 128 here is just an example. How many ranks should be used in your calculation example depends on the number of blocks in Decomp/, Restart/, runtime_mesh/, and server resources. Don’t increase the rank arbitrarily just because the server has more cores. If this preflight needs to prepare the old Restart to the new runtime_mesh, the C++ coast_remap backend will be used by default. The Python reference is only used when --remap-backend python-reference is explicitly added; there is no silent fallback when the C++ backend is not found.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 5.3 What does rank mean? rank is the number in MPI parallel computing, which can be simply understood as “distributing a large calculation to how many parallel workers”. If 128 ranks are used, COAST typically starts 128 parallel processes, numbered 0 to 127. The common three-digit number in the file name is this number, for example: Restart/restart.000 Restart/restart.001 ... Restart/restart.127 rank is not a calculation of accuracy level, nor is the bigger the better. It is strongly related to the calculation case partitioning: Decomp/grid_vv.* represents old style chunking information; runtime_mesh/block_*.dat represents runtime mesh blocking; Restart/restart.NNN represents a continued calculation data saved by each rank; Visit/solution.<step>.domain.<rank>.vtk represents a block of results output by each rank. The most important rules for beginners are: When running for the first time, use the prepared rank number of the template or calculation example; When continuing the calculation, try to use the same rank number as when writing Restart; As many ranks as there are in Restart/restart.NNN, the number of ranks is usually used when continuing the calculation; If there is restart_pdf.NNN, its number must be the same as restart.NNN; When in doubt, run doctor and mesh status first, and do not blindly change --ranks. For example, there are a total of 128 files in Restart/ from restart.000 to restart.127, so when continuing the calculation, you should usually use: bin/coastctl run --case-dir EXEC.demo --ranks 128 --preflight --write --json If you change it to 64 or 256, the program may not be able to correctly read the existing Restart. At worst, it may fail to start, or at worst, it may read mismatched data.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 5.4 What are Restart and PDF Restart? Restart can be translated as “restart” or “continue file”. It is not a result graph for people to see, but an archive for COAST to continue its calculations in the future. A long calculation may take a long time, and the state needs to be saved in the middle; you can continue from the saved state next time instead of restarting from the initial moment. There are two types of common COAST restart files. The first type is flow field Restart: EXEC.demo/Restart/restart.000 EXEC.demo/Restart/restart.001 ... It saves the main flow field data of each rank, such as velocity, pressure-related state, temperature-related state, etc. Newbies to the specific fields do not need to understand them one by one, as long as they know that it determines “where to continue the calculation.” The second category is PDF Restart: EXEC.demo/Restart/restart_pdf.000 EXEC.demo/Restart/restart_pdf.001 ... PDF Restart is related to PDF equations and combustion/mixing related random field states. It can be understood as “the continued calculation state of the combustion and mixing model itself”. If the corresponding model is enabled for the calculation case, it usually needs to be saved and read when the calculation is officially continued. There are usually several sets of important switches in input.d: true true /restart, write to restart ... true true /read_pdf,write_pdf The specific format of this type of line depends on your template, but the meaning is roughly: read_restart: Whether to read the existing Restart/restart.NNN during startup; write_restart: whether to write a new Restart/restart.NNN during operation; read_pdf: Whether to read the existing Restart/restart_pdf.NNN when starting; write_pdf: Whether to write a new Restart/restart_pdf.NNN during operation. Common combinations are as follows. Scenario read_restart write_restart read_pdf write_pdf Description Start short test from initial conditions false true false Depends on the study Do not read the old state, but can write the new one Restart Continue calculation from existing flow field without PDF Restart true true false true Common in the case of only cold flow field Restart Resume from fully saved state true true true true restart.NNN and restart_pdf.NNN are both complete Only check startup, don’t want to overwrite the results Don’t run it officially Don’t change it yet Don’t change it yet Don’t change it yet Use --preflight first Note: If there is no restart_pdf.NNN in Restart/, do not set read_pdf to true. Otherwise the program will try to read a PDF Restart that does not exist, and will usually fail to start. You can first set it to read_pdf=false, write_pdf=true to let the program write a new PDF Restart in the new calculation; the calculation will be completely continued from these new files next time. Note: Do not manually copy only part of Restart/restart.NNN. Missing the Restart of any rank may cause the calculation to fail.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 5.5 Short test, formal calculation and continued calculation The operation of COAST is recommended to be carried out in three steps: short test, formal calculation, and continued calculation. The difference between the three is mainly in the number of steps of input.d, the output frequency and whether to read Restart.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 5.5.1 Short test The goal of the short test is to confirm that “the calculation example can be started, can walk a few steps, can write logs, can write Visit, and can write Restart.” Short measurements are not intended to draw final physical conclusions. Before the short test, open EXEC.demo/input.d and change the number of steps and output frequency to be smaller. Notes may vary slightly from template to template, but common key items are: 10 /lstep 1 /stepsave : write restart file interval 1 /stepplot : write plot file interval means: lstep: the maximum number of steps to be calculated; stepsave: write Restart every few steps; stepplot: Write Visit/VTK results every few steps. The short test can be set to 10 steps, 20 steps or 50 steps. In order to quickly confirm the output link, stepsave and stepplot can be set to a smaller value first, such as 1, 5 or 10. The specific value should be combined with the scale of the calculation example. For calculation examples with large grids, it is not recommended to write a large number of results in each step. Check first after modification: bin/coastctl case validate --case-dir EXEC.demo --json bin/coastctl boundary preview --case-dir EXEC.demo --write --json bin/coastctl mesh status --case-dir EXEC.demo --json bin/coastctl run --case-dir EXEC.demo --ranks 128 --preflight --write --json After these are passed, start it: bin/coastctl run --case-dir EXEC.demo --ranks 128 --execute --preflight --write --json Execution location: root directory of the portable package. After execution, you should see: The command quickly returns a piece of JSON, in which "status": "started", and the running manifest and status file are written outside the calculation .coast_run_logs/: .coast_run_logs/<case>/<run>/coast_run.json .coast_run_logs/_state/<case-key>.json Note: This command starts background calculation. The return of the command does not mean that the calculation has been completed, it only means that COAST has started running. Follow up with monitoring commands to confirm the progress.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 5.5.2 Formal calculation After the short test is passed, input.d is changed to the number of steps and output frequency required for formal calculation. Formal calculations usually require attention to two things: Don’t write the wrong order of magnitude in lstep; stepsave and stepplot should not be too small, otherwise the resulting files may be very large. For example: 5000 /lstep 500 /stepsave : write restart file interval 500 /stepplot : write plot file interval This is just an example and does not mean that all calculation cases should be set up this way. If novices do not have clear requirements, it is recommended to first ask the calculation example provider or project leader: how many steps to run, how often to save Restart, and how often to output Visit. Still need to perform before formal calculation: bin/coastctl doctor --case-dir EXEC.demo --json bin/coastctl case validate --case-dir EXEC.demo --json bin/coastctl mesh status --case-dir EXEC.demo --json bin/coastctl run --case-dir EXEC.demo --ranks 128 --preflight --write --json Start after confirming that everything is correct: bin/coastctl run --case-dir EXEC.demo --ranks 128 --execute --preflight --write --json Note: Do not edit input.d, boundary_conditions.d, ibm_mesh.d, runtime_mesh/ or Restart/ during formal calculation. These files are the input and state that the running program depends on, and changes during operation may lead to uninterpretable results.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 5.5.3 Continue calculation To continue the calculation is to continue the calculation from the existing Restart/. Before continuing the calculation, please confirm: The last calculation has been stopped normally, or at least a complete Restart has been written; The number of Restart/restart.NNN is consistent with the number of ranks; If you want to read PDF Restart, the number of Restart/restart_pdf.NNN is also the same; The current meshes corresponding to runtime_mesh/ and Restart are not replaced arbitrarily; read_restart in input.d is turned on; lstep is set to the total number of steps or the number of subsequent steps you want to continue running, and is executed according to the current calculation example; Do --preflight first, then start. Common checks before renewal: bin/coastctl doctor --case-dir EXEC.demo --json bin/coastctl mesh status --case-dir EXEC.demo --json bin/coastctl run --case-dir EXEC.demo --ranks 128 --preflight --write --json Start continuation calculation: bin/coastctl run --case-dir EXEC.demo --ranks 128 --execute --preflight --write --json After execution, view the screen or graphical auxiliary interface monitoring page. If it is a complete continuation, a prompt similar to “Restarting from previous solution” will usually appear in the log; if a PDF Restart is read, a prompt such as “Restarting Pdf Equation from Previous Solution” may also appear. NOTE: Do not delete the old Restart/ before continuation to “save space”. If you must organize space, copy the entire study directory or archive Restart/ and Visit/ to a safe location before proceeding.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 5.6 Using coastctl run coastctl run is the recommended entry point for novices. It helps you generate a running plan, do pre-start checks, start background calculations, and record this running information.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 5.6.1 Only generate plans bin/coastctl run --case-dir EXEC.demo --ranks 128 --write --json Execution location: root directory of the portable package. Meaning: Generate a running plan, but do not check the input and do not start the program. After execution you should see: .coast_run_logs/<case>/<run>/coast_run_plan.json The plan will record: Calculation example directory; rank number; The command that will actually be run; -Standard output log location; -Standard error log location; Whether it is actually executed.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 5.6.2 Do preflight check bin/coastctl run --case-dir EXEC.demo --ranks 128 --preflight --write --json Meaning: Automatically do case validate before starting, and then write the plan, but do not actually run it. This is the most recommended step before official operation. If Restart remapping is involved, this step checks and calls the C++ coast_remap production backend by default. Python reference is only used for explicit diagnostic commands: bin/coastctl run --case-dir EXEC.demo --ranks 128 \ --preflight --remap-backend python-reference --write --json
title: COAST User Manual

content: 5.6.3 Really start the calculation bin/coastctl run --case-dir EXEC.demo --ranks 128 --execute --preflight --write --json Meaning: do preflight first, and then start it in the EXEC.demo directory: mpirun -np 128 ../bin/coast-solver stdout will be written to the external running directory: .coast_run_logs/<case>/<run>/stdout.log stderr will be written to the external running directory: .coast_run_logs/<case>/<run>/stderr.log Running information will be written to the external running directory and external status index: .coast_run_logs/<case>/<run>/coast_run.json .coast_run_logs/_state/<case-key>.json Note: If there is already a running COAST, coastctl run will usually refuse to start again to avoid running two programs in the same calculation directory at the same time. Do not click “Start Run” repeatedly using multiple terminals.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 5.6.4 If coastctl is not used, what is the underlying command? Some developers or old scripts will run directly in the calculation example directory: cd EXEC.demo mkdir -p ../.coast_run_logs/manual mpirun -np 128 ../bin/coast-solver \ > ../.coast_run_logs/manual/EXEC.demo.stdout.log \ 2> ../.coast_run_logs/manual/EXEC.demo.stderr.log This is an ordinary manual low-level startup method; the equivalent command in the source code version is cd EXEC && mpirun -np N ./coast. If MPI size differs from the active runtime mesh rank count, and input.d and Mesh-5 configuration allow startup regrid / restart remap, the startup phase will take the controlled preflight/write/remap path before solver reads fields. If preconditions fail, such as rank, file number, mesh identity, remap backend or gate conditions are not met, the shutdown should fail and the reason should be explained in the screen / JSON diagnostic. It is more recommended for novices and production calculations to use coastctl run, because it will record the plan, check existing runs, unify the log location, and complete prepare/remap/activation through C++ coast_remap when needed. Note: direct mpirun should not leave .log, .json, .pid or session temporary files in the EXEC.demo root directory. When it is necessary to temporarily redirect stdout/stderr, place it in .coast_run_logs/, a temporary directory or a user-specified archive directory outside the calculation. Note: Do not run long studies directly without a limit on the number of steps. Before running, you must confirm that lstep, stepsave, and stepplot in input.d are the values ​​you want.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 5.7 Optional auxiliary: monitor operation with graphical auxiliary interface The graphical auxiliary interface is a graphical interface for novices. They can view the calculation status, edit input, start running, stop running, view Visit output and do basic post-processing in the browser.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 5.7.1 Start the graphical auxiliary interface On the Linux server, enter the root directory of the portable package and execute: bin/coast-ui --workspace "$PWD" --case-dir "$PWD/EXEC.demo" --host 127.0.0.1 --port 18765 After execution, you should see: The graphical auxiliary interface service is running in the terminal and occupies 127.0.0.1:18765. If you use a browser on a Windows computer to access a remote Linux server, you need to do port forwarding in Windows PowerShell: ssh -N -L 18765:127.0.0.1:18765 user@server Replace user@server with your server username and address. This PowerShell window should remain open. Then open it in Windows browser: http://127.0.0.1:18765 Note: 127.0.0.1 means “this machine”. In the server command, it refers to the server itself; in Windows Explorer, it refers to Windows itself. The function of port forwarding is to connect Windows’ 127.0.0.1:18765 to the server’s 127.0.0.1:18765.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 5.7.2 How to view the operation in the graphical auxiliary interface The operation monitoring of the graphical auxiliary interface usually calls: bin/coastctl monitor --case-dir EXEC.demo --json It will read: EXEC.demo/screen .coast_run_logs/<case>/<run>/stdout.log .coast_run_logs/<case>/<run>/stderr.log There are several types of information you can pay attention to: Whether there is currently a screen file; The last recognized step or istep; Whether external stdout.log and stderr.log continue to grow; Whether error summaries such as fatal, mpi error, abort, NaN, Inf etc. appear; Whether there are new result files in Visit/; Whether there is a new continuation file in Restart/. If you do not use a graphical auxiliary interface, you can also execute it in the server terminal: bin/coastctl monitor --case-dir EXEC.demo --json Or look at recent screen logs: tail -80 EXEC.demo/screen Execution location: root directory of the portable package. Note: tail -80 only looks at the last 80 lines and does not modify any files. It’s great for quickly seeing where a program has gone.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 5.8 Gentle Stop Gentle stop means: do not kill the program directly, but tell COAST “Please stop at the appropriate location and try to write the file that should be written.” This is safer than forcing a power off or directly killing the process. Recommended commands: bin/coastctl stop --case-dir EXEC.demo --json Execution location: root directory of the portable package. This command will create in the study directory: EXEC.demo/stop_coast The COAST main program will check this file during operation. If it is found, it will try to stop at the appropriate time and write the corresponding output. After execution, you should see: createdStopFile is shown as true in JSON, and the stopFile path is given. Continue monitoring after stopping: bin/coastctl monitor --case-dir EXEC.demo --json tail -80 EXEC.demo/screen If prompts similar to stop_coast, time > tlast or istep > lstep: stop, finished, or save Restart appear in the log, it means that the program is or has stopped according to the normal process. Note: Gentle Stop does not mean “disappear immediately”. Large calculation examples may not stop until the current step or current output is completed. Do not press Stop and Start continuously within a few seconds. If there is no response after a gentle stop for a long time, and you confirm that it must be ended, you can use a forced stop: bin/coastctl stop --case-dir EXEC.demo --force --json Note: --force will attempt to send a termination signal to the running process, which is more risky than a gentle stop. After a forced stop, check whether Restart/ is complete. You cannot default to the fact that the last result can be continued.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 5.9 Which prompts indicate failure? The following symptoms usually indicate a failure or at least a need to pause the check: coastctl run reports mpirun not found; coastctl run reports missing executable; coastctl run reports that it is already running and active; errorSummary of coastctl monitor is not empty; External stderr.log continues to grow, and MPI error, abort, fatal appear; NaN, Inf, infinity appears in screen; Segmentation fault appears in screen; The log prompts that the restart or restart_pdf file cannot be opened; The log indicates that the boundary configuration is incorrect; Visit/ has no new files for a long time, and screen is no longer updated; The program exits quickly, but does not write the expected Visit or Restart; There is no prompt to read Restart when continuing calculation. When encountering these situations, do not restart repeatedly. Gather information in Chapter 7’s walkthrough order. 6. View and export results The calculation results of COAST are mainly placed in the Visit/ directory. Visit here refers to the VisIt post-processing software, not the English “visit”. COAST will output index files and VTK data files that VisIt can read, helping you view slices, three-dimensional wholes, clouds, contours, and vector maps.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 6.1 What are Visit/solution.visit and chunked VTK files? When a calculation ends or is output, common result files are in: EXEC.demo/Visit/ The most important entry files are usually: EXEC.demo/Visit/solution.visit It is not the complete data itself, but like a “directory listing”. It lists which VTK files VisIt should read. Really large amounts of data are usually found in files like these: EXEC.demo/Visit/solution.00000500.domain.000.vtk EXEC.demo/Visit/solution.00000500.domain.001.vtk ... EXEC.demo/Visit/solution.00000500.domain.127.vtk It can be understood like this: solution: This is the solution result; 00000500: usually represents the 500th step or a certain output step number; domain.000: 0th rank or 0th block; .vtk: a post-processing data format that VisIt can open. If a calculation example is calculated with 128 ranks, then the same output step may correspond to 128 .vtk files. VisIt puts these chunks together into a whole through the .visit file.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 6.2 Why .visit cannot be sent to others alone The .visit file is usually small because it is just an index listing. It might just say: solution.00000500.domain.000.vtk solution.00000500.domain.001.vtk ... If you only send solution.visit to others without sending these .vtk files together, the other party will find that the data is missing when they open it. It’s like sending someone the catalog of a book but not the text. The correct way to share is: send solution.visit; Also sends all solution.<step>.domain.<rank>.vtk it references; Keep the relative path unchanged, preferably still in the same Visit/ folder; If there are multiple output steps, make sure that the .visit and .vtk corresponding to each output step are complete; It is most recommended to use the Visit package download function of the graphical auxiliary interface, so that the system can automatically type the relevant files into a zip. Note: Do not manually select just a few .vtk files to send, unless you know very well that you only want to see certain chunks. Both normal post-processing and archiving should preserve intact chunking.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 6.3 Optional assistance: Download the Visit file using the graphical assistance interface The graphical auxiliary interface will scan the Visit/ directory and classify .visit and .vtk according to data groups. It will internally package the same set of results into a zip to prevent you from missing files. The operation idea is as follows: Start the graphical auxiliary interface; Open http://127.0.0.1:18765 in the browser; Find results, Visit, post-processing or download related pages; View the number of .visit, the number of .vtk and the total size of each set of data; Select the required data group to download; Download a compressed package similar to coast_solution...zip; Keep the Visit/ directory structure after decompression, and then use VisIt to open the .visit file inside. The corresponding download logic of the graphical auxiliary interface will put the .visit and .vtk in the selected group into the zip together. If you select all results, the file may be very large, so you must first confirm that there is enough local disk space. Note: If the graphical auxiliary interface displays vtkCount as 0, it means that it has not found the corresponding VTK data. There is no point in downloading .visit at this time. You should first check whether the calculation actually writes the result.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 6.4 Download and install VisIt VisIt is a commonly used scientific visualization software that can open .visit and .vtk files output by COAST. You can download it from the VisIt official website: https://visit-dav.github.io/visit-website/ Installation suggestions for newbies: Windows users download the Windows version installation package; Linux users can use the system package manager, the cluster installed version, or the official website download version; If the image is automatically generated through the graphical auxiliary interface on the server, the visit command also needs to be found on the server; If VisIt is not in the default path on the server, you can ask the administrator to set COAST_VISIT_BIN to point to the VisIt executable file. Check if VisIt can be found on the server: which visit If there is output from this command, such as /usr/local/bin/visit, it means that the system can find VisIt. If there is no output, the automatic post-processing of the graphical assistant interface may prompt that VisIt cannot be found. Note: VisIt is installed on the local computer to open the downloaded data by itself; VisIt is installed on the server to allow the graphical auxiliary interface to automatically generate images on the server. The two have different uses.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 6.5 Open COAST results in VisIt Take Windows local viewing as an example: Download the Visit zip from the graphical auxiliary interface; Unzip to a directory without Chinese special symbols and a path that is not too deep, such as D:\coast_results\case01; Open VisIt; Select File -> Open file; Find Visit/solution.visit in the unzipped directory; After opening, select the variables and drawing method to be displayed in VisIt; Click on the Draw or similar button to draw. If VisIt says it cannot find certain .vtk files, it is usually because: Only .visit was copied, not .vtk; The directory structure was changed during decompression; The file name was changed by network disk or chat software; Some .vtk are not downloaded completely; The .visit file refers to a relative path, but you separated it from .vtk. Solution: Reuse the graphical auxiliary interface to package and download the complete group, and do not move individual files after decompression.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 6.6 The meaning of common post-processing graphs When novices open VisIt for the first time, they are most likely to be intimidated by the various plot types. It is enough to master the following ones first.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 6.6.1 Pseudocolor: Pseudocolor cloud image A pseudo-color image represents a scalar field in color. For example, areas with high temperatures are displayed in red, and areas with low temperatures are displayed in blue. It’s suitable for viewing: Temperature distribution; pressure distribution; Density distribution; Component concentration; reaction progress; IBM or boundary markers. Operation idea: Add Pseudocolor picture; Select a scalar field; If the internal structure cannot be seen clearly, add Slice slice; Click Draw.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 6.6.2 Slice: slice Slicing is to cut out a plane from the three-dimensional result. It is suitable for viewing internal flow fields because the three-dimensional whole may be obscured by external surfaces. Common slicing directions: slice_x: slice perpendicular to the x direction; slice_y: slice perpendicular to the y direction; slice_z: Slice perpendicular to the z direction. Graphical auxiliary interface These slicing modes are usually provided in automatic post-processing, and are cut at the 50% position by default, which is near the middle.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 6.6.3 3D: three-dimensional whole The three-dimensional whole is suitable for looking at geometric shapes, overall distribution and large-scale structures. However, if the variables mainly change internally, the three-dimensional whole may not be visible clearly, and slicing, transparency or isosurfaces are required.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 6.6.4 Contour: Isoline or isosurface Isolines/isosurfaces represent “where a certain variable is equal to some value.” For example, an area where the temperature is equal to a certain value and an area where the component concentration reaches a certain threshold. It’s suitable for viewing: Approximate position of the flame surface; Boundary of high temperature zone; The position where a certain component reaches a certain concentration; Layered structure of pressure or density.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 6.6.5 Vector: vector image Vector diagrams use arrows to represent direction and magnitude, most commonly velocity vectors. COAST’s graphical auxiliary interface will combine a COAST_velocity vector field when it finds the three velocity components 01_Velocity_U, 01_Velocity_V, and 01_Velocity_W. Vector images are suitable for viewing: direction of flow; return flow area; Jet direction; The speed is generally strong or weak. Note: The arrows will be unclear if they are too dense. You can increase the stride or reduce the number of arrows. Graphical auxiliary interface Automatic diagrams usually use a simplified arrow setup.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 6.7 Optional auxiliary: use graphical auxiliary interface to generate basic post-processing images If VisIt is installed on the server, the graphical auxiliary interface can automatically call VisIt to generate PNG images. It usually does these things: Scan the data group in Visit/; Find available scalar and vector fields; Select Pseudocolor, Contour or Vector; Select slice direction or 3D perspective; Call visit -nowin -cli to generate images in the background; Save the image to Visit/postprocess/. The generated image is usually located at: EXEC.demo/Visit/postprocess/ If the graphical assistant interface prompts: VisIt executable not found; set COAST_VISIT_BIN or install visit Explanation VisIt cannot be found on the server. The solution is to install VisIt, or ask your administrator to set it up: export COAST_VISIT_BIN=/path/to/visit Then restart the graphical assistant interface.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 6.8 Saving images in VisIt If you are viewing the results in the VisIt graphical interface, the general steps for saving an image are: Adjust variables, slices, color range and viewing angle; Select File -> Set save options; Select the image format, such as PNG; Set the resolution, such as 1280 x 900 or 1920 x 1080; Select the save directory; Click Save window. When saving images, it is recommended that the file name contain: Calculation example name; Output the number of steps; variable name; Figure type; Slicing direction. For example: case01_step05000_temperature_slice_y.png case01_step05000_velocity_vector_slice_z.png In this way, when you look back later, you can know the meaning of the picture without opening VisIt.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 6.9 Results Archiving Recommendations A complete and reviewable results archive should contain at least: input.d used this time; boundary_conditions.d used this time; ibm_mesh.d used this time; vtk_output.d used this time; screen; External stdout.log, stderr.log reported by coastctl monitor; The corresponding coast_run.json or coast_run_plan.json in .coast_run_logs/; Visit/solution.visit and corresponding .vtk that need to be reviewed; If the calculation needs to be continued later, complete Restart/; Pictures in Visit/postprocess/ if GUI postprocessing is used. Note: Visit/ is for people to see the results, Restart/ is for the program to continue calculations. The two have different uses and cannot be substituted for each other. Only Visit/ cannot be continued, and only Restart/ cannot directly view the complete regular results in VisIt. 7. Troubleshooting common problems When you encounter a problem, don’t panic or modify many files repeatedly. The most important thing for troubleshooting is to keep the scene: logs, input files, run plans, and result directories. Most of the clues to COAST common problems can be found in the external stdout/stderr logs reported by screen, coastctl monitor, doctor and monitor.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 7.1 General troubleshooting sequence It is recommended to collect information in the following order every time.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 7.1.1 See doctor bin/coastctl doctor --case-dir EXEC.demo --json If there are already failed items here, they will be processed first. For example, mpirun does not exist, the main solver is not executable, and the number of Restart does not match, these are all problems that should be solved before starting.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 7.1.2 View monitor bin/coastctl monitor --case-dir EXEC.demo --json Highlights: Whether screenExists is true; Whether lastStep has grown; Whether stdoutBytes and stderrBytes are abnormal; Whether errorSummary has content.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 7.1.3 View recent logs tail -120 EXEC.demo/screen Execution location: root directory of the portable package. The actual path to stdout/stderr is as reported by bin/coastctl monitor --case-dir EXEC.demo --json, usually under .coast_run_logs/. If a file does not exist, the program may not have written to it, or the startup phase failed. Absence itself is also a clue.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 7.1.4 View key input files sed -n '1,220p' EXEC.demo/input.d sed -n '1,260p' EXEC.demo/boundary_conditions.d Execution location: root directory of the portable package. This step is not to let novices understand all the parameters, but to confirm whether there have been any obvious mistakes recently: whether the number of steps is outrageous, whether the Restart switch matches the file, whether the boundary coordinate range is written incorrectly, and whether the species name is misspelled.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 7.1.5 Pause modifications and sort out problem descriptions If you need to contact a developer or administrator, it is recommended to provide: Calculation example directory name; the order you execute; rank number; Which files have been modified recently; doctor output; monitor output; Last 120 lines of external stderr.log reported by coastctl monitor; Last 120 lines of external stdout.log reported by coastctl monitor; last 120 lines of screen; Whether it can be reproduced, that is, whether it fails again when running again. Note: Don’t just say “It can’t be calculated anymore”. Without logs, it is difficult for others to determine whether it is an input problem, an MPI problem, a grid problem, a boundary problem, or a numerical divergence.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 7.2 Graphical auxiliary interface cannot be connected
title: COAST User Manual

content: Phenomenon Browser opens: http://127.0.0.1:18765 But it shows that it cannot be accessed, the connection is refused, the page keeps spinning, or it cannot be opened.
title: COAST User Manual

content: Common reasons bin/coast-ui is not started on the Linux server; The graphical auxiliary interface has exited after startup; port is not 18765; SSH port forwarding for Windows PowerShell is not left open; The SSH login is not the same server; Server firewall or security policy blocks the connection; You confused the meaning of 127.0.0.1; The browser accesses http, but it is copied to another address; The port is occupied by other programs.
title: COAST User Manual

content: Processing steps Restart the GUI on the Linux server: bin/coast-ui --workspace "$PWD" --case-dir "$PWD/EXEC.demo" --host 127.0.0.1 --port 18765 Do not close this terminal. Then execute in Windows PowerShell: ssh -N -L 18765:127.0.0.1:18765 user@server Don’t close the PowerShell window either. Then the browser opens: http://127.0.0.1:18765 If it still cannot be opened, try another port, for example on the server: bin/coast-ui --workspace "$PWD" --case-dir "$PWD/EXEC.demo" --host 127.0.0.1 --port 18766 Windows PowerShell： ssh -N -L 18766:127.0.0.1:18766 user@server Browser: http://127.0.0.1:18766 Note: Do not use --host 0.0.0.0 lightly. It causes the service to listen on more network addresses and is only suitable for trusted private networks or firewall-protected environments.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 7.3 Port forwarding failed
title: COAST User Manual

content: Phenomenon Execute in PowerShell: ssh -N -L 18765:127.0.0.1:18765 user@server An error is reported later, or the command seems to be running but the browser cannot be opened.
title: COAST User Manual

content: Common reasons user@server is written incorrectly; SSH password, key or springboard settings are incorrect; Windows local 18765 port has been occupied; The GUI on the server is not running on 18765; The server’s SSH configuration disables port forwarding; Company or campus network restricts SSH; The PowerShell window is closed and the forwarding is disconnected.
title: COAST User Manual

content: Processing steps First confirm that ordinary SSH can log in: ssh user@server If you cannot log in through ordinary SSH, first solve the account, network or key issues. If normal SSH can log in, but port forwarding fails, change a local port: ssh -N -L 18766:127.0.0.1:18765 user@server The meaning of this command is: Windows uses 18766 locally, and the server is still connected to 18765. The browser should open: http://127.0.0.1:18766 If the server graphical auxiliary interface is also changed to 18766, write 18766 on both sides: ssh -N -L 18766:127.0.0.1:18766 user@server Note: -N means forwarding only and not opening the remote shell. It may not produce any output when running normally and appear to be “stuck”, but it is actually maintaining the tunnel. Do not close this window.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 7.4 mpirun is not started or cannot be found
title: COAST User Manual

content: Phenomenon coastctl run reports error: mpirun not found Or the mpirun check in doctor failed.
title: COAST User Manual

content: Reason COAST relies on MPI for parallel operation. mpirun is a command to start multiple ranks. If the system cannot find mpirun, COAST cannot be started in parallel mode.
title: COAST User Manual

content: Processing steps Check on the server: which mpirun If there is no output, MPI cannot be found in the current environment. You can: Confirm whether the cluster module needs to be loaded first, such as module load... provided by the administrator; Confirm whether the environment script of the portable package needs to be executed first; Contact the administrator to install or configure MPI; Do not install multiple MPI versions and mix them at will. If which mpirun has output but the operation still fails, first use monitor to find the external stderr.log: bin/coastctl monitor --case-dir EXEC.demo --json Common reasons include a mismatch between the MPI version and the program compilation environment, insufficient server resources, and the operating system does not allow running directly on the login node. In a cluster environment, it may be necessary to submit through the job scheduling system instead of mpirun directly.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 7.5 Restart quantity and rank do not match
title: COAST User Manual

content: Phenomenon The calculation fails during continuation, or the doctor prompt is similar to: pdf=64 restart=128 decomp=64 restart=128 You may also see in the log that a certain restart.NNN or restart_pdf.NNN cannot be opened.
title: COAST User Manual

content: Reason Each rank requires its own Restart file. For example, if you use 128 ranks to continue the calculation, you usually need: Restart/restart.000 ... Restart/restart.127 If you also want to read PDF Restart, you also need: Restart/restart_pdf.000 ... Restart/restart_pdf.127 As long as one is missing, the numbers are not consecutive, and the quantities are inconsistent, the program may fail.
title: COAST User Manual

content: Processing steps First count the number of files: find EXEC.demo/Restart -maxdepth 1 -name 'restart.[0-9][0-9][0-9]' | wc -l find EXEC.demo/Restart -maxdepth 1 -name 'restart_pdf.[0-9][0-9][0-9]' | wc -l Execution location: root directory of the portable package. If restart.NNN is 128 and restart_pdf.NNN is 0, it means you may only have flow field Restart and no PDF Restart. Do not read PDF Restart at this time. Set read_pdf in input.d to false, but you can leave write_pdf as true and let the next section calculate and write a new PDF Restart. If restart.NNN is 128 and restart_pdf.NNN is 64, don’t force it. You need to retrieve the complete PDF Restart, or confirm whether you can regenerate it without reading the PDF Restart. If the number of restart.NNN is inconsistent with your planned --ranks, do not randomly delete files to “make up the quantity”. When you need to change the rank number or switch to a new runtime mesh, first use coastctl run --preflight; the production path defaults to writing staging through C++ coast_remap, and then controlled activation determines whether to replace active Restart/runtime_mesh. Note: Changing from 128 rank to 64 rank does not mean simply deleting half of the files. That involves re-blocking or remapping, which is an advanced operation and requires developer confirmation.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 7.6 Visit file is incomplete
title: COAST User Manual

content: Phenomenon VisIt reports an error after opening .visit, or only displays a part of the area, or a certain set of results in the graphical auxiliary interface shows that .visit is present but the number of .vtk is obviously wrong.
title: COAST User Manual

content: Common reasons Visit/ was copied before the calculation was finished; Only .visit was downloaded, not .vtk; The .vtk of some ranks is not written; Interruption during file copying; The disk is full, causing some results to be unfinished; You mixed .visit and .vtk from different calculation examples; The program exited abnormally during output.
title: COAST User Manual

content: Processing steps First look at the Visit group of the graphical auxiliary interface to confirm whether vtkCount is reasonable. The command line can also be roughly checked: find EXEC.demo/Visit -maxdepth 1 -name '*.visit' | wc -l find EXEC.demo/Visit -maxdepth 1 -name '*.vtk' | wc -l If you know the rank number and the number of output steps, you can estimate the number of .vtk. For example, 128 rank, 1 output step, usually there are at least 128 corresponding solution.<step>.domain.<rank>.vtk. Check the .visit reference content: sed -n '1,80p' EXEC.demo/Visit/solution.visit If the .vtk file listed there does not exist in the directory, the result is incomplete. Package and download from the graphical auxiliary interface again, or wait for the calculation to stop completely and confirm that the file is written before copying. Note: Do not treat incomplete Visits as physical anomalies. It starts with a file integrity issue.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 7.7 Boundary selection is empty
title: COAST User Manual

content: Phenomenon After running boundary preview, it is found that no boundary is selected for an entrance, exit or wall, or an error related to boundary configuration is reported soon after running.
title: COAST User Manual

content: Common reasons The coordinate range in boundary_conditions.d is written incorrectly; axis, side, bounds and other selectors are inconsistent with the actual geometric direction; Misunderstanding of geometric units, such as mistaking millimeters for meters; The inlet position is inside the solid, not on the outer boundary of the fluid; source ibmSurface is used, but the corresponding IBM adjacent fluid surface does not exist; The patch name or STL tag does not exist; Boundaries were not rechecked after modifying the mesh.
title: COAST User Manual

content: Processing steps First generate a border preview: bin/coastctl boundary preview --case-dir EXEC.demo --write --json View the boundary file: sed -n '1,260p' EXEC.demo/boundary_conditions.d If you use coordinates to select boundaries, focus on checking: Whether the coordinate axis direction is correct; Are the minimum and maximum values reversed? Whether the numerical units are consistent with the geometry; Whether the selection range actually covers the boundary surface; Whether the internal area was selected by mistake. If you’re not sure about a geometric location, use the grid/IBM preview feature to check it first instead of guessing the coordinates. Note: Do not directly expand to the entire domain when the boundary is empty. Wrong selection of the entrance, exit, and wall will make the calculation results meaningless. Even if the program can run, it does not mean it is correct.
title: COAST User Manual

content: 7.8 Calculation failed or stopped early Failure to calculate is not necessarily the same kind of problem. According to major categories, they can be divided into configuration problems, operating environment problems, grid/boundary problems, spray model problems, numerical divergence problems, etc.
